action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
GitHub won't let one account own both a repo and its fork:

```
failed to fork: winksaville/vc-x1-forktest cannot be forked. A single user account cannot own both a parent and fork.
```

So `winksaville/vc-x1-original` as a fork of `winksaville/vc-x1` isn't possible. That's a change to the plan, so I've stopped here.

The plan needs a fork, not just a copy, because of the agent-repo. Agent commits are never rewritten, so their `ocid:` URLs will keep naming the old work SHAs at `github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<old-sha>`. A fork shares GitHub's object store, so as long as the fork's `main` holds the old commits, those URLs should keep resolving on vc-x1 itself. A plain copy keeps the old commits too, but only at its own URL, and the old URLs on vc-x1 would depend on GitHub never cleaning up the unreachable commits.

The ways forward:

1. **Fork into an organization.** You're a member of `01alchemist`, `zenlang`, `AletheiaWareLLC`, `kendallstaking`, `crab-cad` and `IDEKALang`. You could also create a new one, such as `winksaville-archive`. The fork would be `<org>/vc-x1-original`, and the old URLs should keep working through the fork network. This is the one I'd test.
2. **A pushed copy, `winksaville/vc-x1-original`, outside the fork network.** The old commits live at the new name. Old links on vc-x1 work only as long as GitHub keeps unreachable commits, which isn't guaranteed.
3. **Keep the old main in vc-x1 under a non-branch ref,** such as `refs/archive/old-main`. Whether GitHub accepts and keeps a custom ref like that needs testing. A normal `jj git clone` wouldn't fetch it, so it wouldn't cause the divergence the tag did.

To go with 1, tell me which organization, or create the new one, and run the fork yourself if it's refused for me:

```
! gh repo fork winksaville/vc-x1-forktest --org <org> --fork-name vc-x1-forktest-original --clone=false
```

I'll then rewrite the three descriptions locally, you force-push, and I run the step-4 checks. The test repo `winksaville/vc-x1-forktest` exists with the three commits pushed.

The rung-1 review is still waiting for your "continue".

The plain version: GitHub won't let you fork your own repo into your own account. For the old links to keep working, the fork has to live in an organization, or we keep the old commits under a hidden ref in vc-x1 itself. Pick one and we carry on with the test.

A sure answer would need a second throwaway repo, force-pushed the same way without a fork, then compared after GitHub has had time to clean up.

- The fork depends on the `inksaville` account. Deleting that account, or the fork, removes the thing keeping the old commits reachable.
- The fork has to be made after the backfill's local run and before its force-push, just as here.

content.text:
Nothing changed on the fork. The SHAs changed on winksaville, and that was the point of the test:

- **`inksaville/...-original` at `36caa9ce`:** the fork was taken before the rewrite, so it holds the original commits unchanged.
- **`winksaville/vc-x1-forktest` at `83dd64d0`:** I rewrote the three descriptions there and force-pushed. A git SHA is a hash that covers the commit message, so changing a description gives a new SHA. That's also why the real backfill changes every work SHA.

So "feat: three" now exists as two commits: the old one, kept by the fork, and the rewritten one on winksaville's `main`.

**Why the edited URL works.** GitHub stores a repo and all its forks in one shared object store, called the fork network. Any commit in the network can be shown at any repo's URL, even if that repo's branches don't contain it. The banner you saw is GitHub saying exactly that: "does not belong to any branch on this repository, and may belong to a fork outside of the repository."

That surprising behavior is what the fork scheme relies on:
- Agent commits are never rewritten.
- So after the backfill, their `ocid:` trailers still say `github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<old-sha>`.
- Those links keep opening because `inksaville/vc-x1-original` keeps the old commits in the network. You'd see that same banner.

The one caveat from before still stands. Right after a force-push, GitHub would also show an unreachable commit for a while even with no fork. The fork is what should keep these links working long after that.

The plain version: the rewrite made new SHAs on winksaville, and the fork kept the old ones. GitHub lets you open the fork's old commits through winksaville's URL, and the banner marks them. That's why old links in the agent-repo will keep working after the real backfill.

content.text:
You're right in general: git garbage-collects a commit once no ref points to it. Here, though, every old commit still has a ref, on both sides.

**Locally, jj holds them.** `gitk --all` draws every ref, and this repo has more than branches:

```
refs/heads/main                  83dd64d   the rewritten tip
refs/remotes/origin/main         83dd64d
refs/jj/keep/36caa9ce…           the old "feat: three"
refs/jj/keep/0a0ff685…           the old "feat: two"
refs/jj/keep/57778e49…           the old "feat: one"
refs/jj/keep/…                   (16 more)
```

- jj writes a `refs/jj/keep/<sha>` for every commit it creates or sees, so that `jj undo` and the operation log can always return to it. Those refs keep git's gc away from the old tree.
- The other `keep` refs are the in-between states from my three `jj describe` calls, one rewrite per call, plus the working-copy commits. That's why gitk shows more than two clean trees.
- They're removed only when you prune old operations yourself (`jj op abandon ..<op>`, then `jj util gc`). jj never does it on its own.

**On GitHub, the fork holds them.**
- `jj git push` sends bookmarks only, never `refs/jj/keep/*`. So `winksaville/vc-x1-forktest` really has no ref to the old commits; its only branch is `main` at `83dd64d`.

The work-repo's `pcid:` trailers don't need the old commits. In the rehearsal's fresh clone, all 686 rewritten commits have `pcid:` trailers naming their actual new parents, with no mismatches. The rewrite runs parent-first, so each commit's `pcid:` is set from its parent's new SHA. Everything a work `pcid:` names is reachable from `main`, as long as `main` exists.

The old SHAs are named only by the agent-repo's `ocid:` trailers, since agent commits are never rewritten. Those are the links the fork has to keep alive.

**Do they have an internal reference?** Yes, though not inside winksaville's repo. It's `refs/heads/main` in `inksaville/vc-x1-original`. We think GitHub collects garbage per fork network: an object stays while any repo in the network can reach it. That fits what we saw: winksaville's URL showed the old commit and served it to `git fetch` by SHA. GitHub's own guidance on removing sensitive data warns that commits stay reachable through forks for this reason.

**That makes it as permanent as the fork, which isn't forever.** The old links break if:
- the fork is deleted, or the `inksaville` account is;
- the fork's `main` is force-pushed or deleted;
- the fork leaves the network. GitHub does this when the parent changes visibility, for example vc-x1 going private and back.
- GitHub changes its policy. We'd have no say.

The first two are under your control. Two ways to make them safer:
1. **Branch protection on the fork's `main`,** blocking force-pushes and deletion. A slip on `inksaville` then can't drop the commits.
2. **A copy outside GitHub.** Your local vc-x1 keeps the old tree under `refs/jj/keep/*`, but only until you prune the operation log. A bare mirror (`git clone --mirror` of the fork) on a disk you back up would let the history be pushed back if the network ever lost it, and the SHAs would come back identical.

The only way to make the agent links independent of GitHub would be rewriting the agent commits too. That breaks the rule that keeps agent SHAs stable, and it would move the problem, not remove it.

The plain version: the work-repo's links all point at the new commits, which `main` keeps. Only the agent-repo's links point at old commits, and those depend on the fork. The fork is a real reference that GitHub honors, but it's only as permanent as the `inksaville` account and that repo. Protect the fork's `main`, and keep a backed-up mirror if you want a guarantee that doesn't depend on GitHub.

You're right, and I was wrong. The real agent-repo has no `ocid:` trailers:

```
agent main: commits=651 ochid-lines=702 ocid-lines=0 pcid-lines=0
```

The links run this way:

| Trailer | Carried by | Names | After the backfill |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ochid:` | Agent commits | A work **change id** | Still valid. jj keeps the change id when it rewrites a commit (both test records above carry `change-id yyplsvuv…`). |
| `ochid:` | Work commits | An agent change id | Still valid. Agent commits aren't touched. |
| `ocid:` | Work commits | An agent **SHA** URL | Valid, and agent SHAs never change. |
| `pcid:` | Work commits | Parent work SHA URLs | Rewritten to the new parents; all 686 match. |

So nothing in either repo names an old work SHA after the backfill. The links between the repos don't depend on the old commit records. The fresh-clone rehearsal showed that too: validate-desc found only the known list.

That changes what the fork is for. It keeps old work SHAs alive only for references from outside the repos' trailers, such as:
- links already posted somewhere, like the `winksaville/vc-x1/commit/ffa3ba13…` link you pasted earlier;
- SHAs written in file content, like the short SHAs in `TODO.md` and `notes/` or in commit bodies;
- your bookmarks and old clones.

Without the fork, those would eventually stop resolving on GitHub. Nothing that lookup or validate-desc depends on would break. The fork is still cheap insurance, but it's a convenience, not a requirement for correctness. That makes branch protection on the fork optional.

When I update the cycle-record I'll state the fork's role that way. I'll also check that the deliberation doesn't repeat my mistake about agent `ocid:`s.

The plain version: you're right. The agent-repo links to work commits by change id, and jj keeps change ids through the rewrite, so every link between the repos survives on its own. The fork only keeps old commit links from outside the repos working, like ones in old notes or pasted elsewhere.

```

The confusion is ours: we've been saying "fork" loosely, while a GitHub fork means the whole history, shared. What we built is a new root commit holding vc-x1's tree, plus a note naming the vc-x1 commit it came from.

That's also better than a literal `--depth 1` clone:

| | Shallow clone (`--depth 1`) | New root commit (the test) |
|---|---|---|
| Root commit | vc-x1's own commit, same SHA, with a missing parent marked as shallow | A new commit with no parent |
| Push to a new GitHub repo | We think GitHub refuses a push from a shallow repo into an empty repo | A normal push |
| Link back to vc-x1 | Implicit (the same SHA), and fragile | Explicit, in the root's description |
| Duplicated history | None | None |

What it costs is what the test found. `git log`, `git blame`, and lookup in vc-x2 all stop at the root, and anything older means looking in vc-x1. That's what the rung-2 findings are for: a trailer on the root naming the vc-x1 commit, and lookup following it across.

Two corrections for the real vc-x2, since the test root was made before the backfill was settled:
- The root should name vc-x1's final commit after the backfill. The test names `a99342879689` from the first rehearsal.
- The URL should be `https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1`, not a `file://` path.

I'd also stop calling it a fork, in the record and in the trailer we file. Something like "vc-x2 starts from vc-x1's tree", with a `seeded-from:` trailer, can't be confused with a GitHub fork. Tell me if you prefer another word; otherwise I'll use "seeded from" when I write the rung-2 subsection.

The plain version: the test vc-x2 already has no history, just one commit holding vc-x1's files and a note pointing back to vc-x1. That's better than a shallow clone, which GitHub may refuse to push. The "fork" in its title was loose wording, and I'd rename the idea to "seeded from" so it isn't mistaken for a GitHub fork.

Not `cp -r`. The transcript shows these steps:

1. **Export the tree:** from the first rehearsal's fresh clone, `git archive main | tar -x -C ~/tmp/x2t/vc-x2`. That gives exactly the tracked files of vc-x1's `main`. It leaves out `.git`, `.jj`, `.agent-session`, and ignored files like `target/` and `tmp/`, which `cp -r` would have copied.
2. **Rename the config:** `sed` in `.vc-config.md`, changing `vc-x1.agent-session` to `vc-x2.agent-session` and the member name `vc-x1` to `vc-x2`.
3. **Make the root commit:** `git init -b main`, `git add -A`, then `git commit` with "feat: vc-x2 forks vc-x1 without history" and the "Forked from vc-x1 a99342879689…" note.
4. **Adopt:** `vc-x1 init --target ./vc-x2 --test-repo remotes --adopt`. It refused the tracked dual config, so I moved my edited `.vc-config.md` aside to `~/tmp/x2t/vc-config-x2.md` and amended the root commit without it. The adopt then:
   - created `.agent-session` and the two bare remotes;
   - wrote a default `.vc-config.md`;
   - made the "Adopt as a dual-repo workspace" commit;
   - created the `~/.claude/projects/` symlink.

One consequence: vc-x2's root tree is vc-x1's tree minus `.vc-config.md`, so its tree SHA differs from vc-x1's. The config came back in the adopt commit as the default, not my renamed one. That's one of the adopt frictions filed for rung 2.

For the real vc-x2 I'd keep steps 1 and 3, `git archive` from vc-x1's post-backfill `main`, then a new root commit. Once adopt is fixed to accept a renamed config, the root would hold vc-x1's whole tree with only the config changed.

The plain version: not a plain copy. I exported only the files vc-x1's `main` tracks, committed them as a single first commit in a new repo, then ran vc-x1's adopt to add the agent-repo and the remotes. Adopt rejected my edited config, so that one file differs from the plan.

content.text:
Yes, it's equivalent. `cp -r`, then deleting `.git`, `.jj`, `.agent-session`, and the ignored files (`target/`, `tmp/`, `tmp-durable/`, …), then the edits and the adopt, ends in the same place.

I used `git archive` because it does the deletes for you. It copies exactly the files `main` tracks, at the committed version, so there's no list of what to remove and nothing gets missed. It also ignores any uncommitted edits in the source working copy. With `cp -r`, the result depends on the source directory's state, and a forgotten untracked file goes into vc-x2's root commit.

Both lead to the same next step: `git init`, one commit, then adopt.

The plain version: yes, the result is the same. `git archive` just does the cleanup automatically by copying only what vc-x1 has committed, which makes it harder to bring something extra along.

content.text:
That's consistent with the two work commits on the known list, `ltwkxykzutws` and `lxonplwlulwq`. If you made them by hand, they belong there as "a commit made outside the agent, by design" rather than as a defect. I can reword their reason in `notes/vc-x1-history.md`.

On the trailers, `agent-data/jj.md` and the rationale give each one's reason. Here's what each buys and costs:

**`ocid:` (the agent SHA, on work commits)**
- What it buys:
  - One click from a work commit on GitHub to its agent commit, which is the link you hovered and copied.
  - It resolves with plain git, no jj needed.
  - It pins the agent commit's exact content, since a SHA is a hash: the transcript the link names can't change without the link going stale.
- What it costs is what you describe:
  - Agent commits can never be amended or squashed into ("nothing folds into a commit an `ocid:` names").
  - Commit order is forced: agent first, or the `xxxx` placeholder plus `trailers --update` before publishing.
  - A mid-cycle backup takes three commands.

  Without it, a squash-push of the agent-repo after you exit me keeps the agent commit's change id, so every `ochid:` naming it still resolves.

**`pcid:` (parent SHAs, on work commits)**
- The rationale gives it two jobs:
  - "A commit cannot hold its own SHA, so a parent's is what names the work-repo at a real commit." That is, it records which repo a commit lives in.
  - "It still says where a forked commit came from", if it's cherry-picked or copied elsewhere.
- Within the repo it duplicates git's own parent pointers, and GitHub already shows parents.
- Its cost is the cascade: a child's description contains its parent's SHA, so changing any commit's description forces a rewrite of everything above it. That's why the backfill must go parent-first, and part of why it took 36 minutes.
- Its second job is exactly what vc-x2's root needs, but that's one `seeded-from:` trailer on one commit, not a line on every commit.

**Your proposal, `ochid:` plus the agent-repo's URL.** A form for it already exists: jj.md says a published `<repo-url>#<chid>` stays valid. What it can't do is take a GitHub click to the commit, because GitHub doesn't know jj change ids and the `#<chid>` fragment lands on the repo's front page. We think a GitHub commit-search link for the work change id in the agent-repo would find the agent commit, since that commit's `ochid:` names it. We haven't tested that.

**The consequence for this cycle is big.** The backfill exists to add `ocid:` and `pcid:` to 659 commits. If both go away, vc-x1 needs no rewrite: the old SHAs stay valid, and there's no fork scheme and no force-push of `main`. "Complete" becomes `ochid:`s validated plus the known list.

My recommendation:
1. Let rung 1 land as reviewed. Its code is useful either way: older-id normalization, validate-desc notes, the dry run and summary, and the known list.
2. Hold the real backfill, which runs after the Land anyway, until you've decided on the trailers.
3. Make the trailer change a cycle of its own, since it changes `vc-x1 commit`, `trailers`, validate-desc, and the agent-files. This cycle could then close without a rewrite.

Tell me how you want to proceed. The rung-1 review is still open.

The plain version: `ocid:` gives a one-click GitHub link and pins the transcript's exact content, but it's also what stops you cleaning up the agent-repo and forces the commit order. `pcid:` mostly repeats what git already knows, and it's why rewriting history is slow. Dropping both would mean vc-x1 doesn't need its history rewritten at all. I'd land this rung, hold the backfill, and decide the trailers as a separate cycle.

Agreed. A malformed trailer in history can't be fixed for free: rewriting a published commit changes its SHA and the SHAs of everything above it. That's why the history gets a known list and not repairs, and why the cheap fix is to stop bad values getting in at `@`.

Good that jj stopped it. Nothing changed: jj refuses an immutable commit before it rewrites anything. Commits on `main@origin` are immutable by default, and `mkqtvoknqzlp` is published.

The hint shows the real cost: "This operation would rewrite 571 immutable commits." That's every agent commit above it. With today's trailers, each of those 571 gets a new SHA, and every work `ocid:` naming one of them goes stale. Your proposal changes exactly this: with `ochid:` alone, those 571 keep their change ids, and the fix costs only a force-push of the agent-repo.

The one way past the protection is `--ignore-immutable`. I used it only in the throwaway test repos, and on the real repos it falls under the rule against re-describing published commits without coordinating first.

The plain version: no harm done. jj refused because the commit is published and changing it would have rewritten the 571 agent commits after it. That number is the cost of fixing old history under today's trailers, and dropping `ocid:` would make it far smaller.

content.text:
That answers it, and it corrects what I said earlier. **None of the eleven is work on another repo.** All are vc-x1 work commits from two cycles whose rungs never reached `main`. Finding them was easy, because the transcripts record exactly what you guessed. Each `vc-x1 push` printed lines like:

```
push message: title="…", work_chid=ulnvkqsqkmrs, bot_chid=mmxnuskzyqvt, …
push commit-work: commit -R /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1
push push-work: git push --bookmark agent-filesadoption-from-iiac-perf-zc-ring-x1-2026-08-31 …
```

That gives the repo, the work change id, and the bookmark. In all eleven, the `ochid:` was already correct; it names a work commit that isn't on `main`.

| Cycle | Agent commits | What happened to the work side |
|---|---|---|
| "feat: the family directory", bookmark `feat-the-family-directory`, 2026-10-16 | 6 | Never landed, and the bookmark was deleted. **The commits still exist locally** (`d0c39688`, `b052cb90`, …) in jj's operation history, and at that operation each one names its agent partner correctly. |
| "agent-files(adoption): from iiac-perf, zc-ring-x1, 2026-08-31", its own bookmark | 5 | We think the ladder was squashed when it landed, as `oxqznutxpxvs` on `main`, before the "never squashed" rule. Its title is the bare cycle title, and a squash keeps one change id and drops the rest. The rungs are gone locally, and the operation log only goes back to 2026-09-28. |

So the second cycle is a live example of why the rule says a ladder is never squashed.

**How hard is it in general?** For any agent commit whose session used `vc-x1 push`, it's mechanical: the transcript names the repo path and the work change id. A tool could do the search I just did by hand. Where it falls short is when the work commit no longer exists, as with the five squashed rungs. Then the repo and id are known, but there's nothing left to link to.

# vc-x1's history: the links that do not resolve

The known list of the cycle **chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2**: every commit in vc-x1's
history whose link to its partner cannot be made to resolve, with why. After the whole-history
`vc-x1 trailers --update`, `vc-x1 validate-desc` over a fresh clone reports an `err` or a `miss`
for these and for nothing else. Each is named by its change id, which the rewrite keeps, since
every work SHA changes. An agent commit's SHA does not, the agent-repo never being rewritten.

Found by the rehearsal of 2026-11-06, in a fresh clone of the rehearsal's remotes.

## Errors

### The work-repo

- `mnonktwnuywp` 2026-07-08 chore: prep pin-bot-to-main cycle (0.68.0-0): its `ochid:` names
  `mzovqnqsmnlk`, which is in no agent-repo, the original's included.

### The agent-repo

The partner is in no repo searched, the work-repo nor the `vc-x1-family`, `vc-x1-template`, and
`vc-x1-messages` siblings. We think each was made in another family member's work-repo while this
agent-repo recorded the session: the family directory and the agent-files adoption were family
work.

- `opqrntkrtxrk` 2026-10-17 feat: the family directory closing, naming `uwsznqssswzt`

  `psywsvrqluxo`
- `xmkzlkvlsuuq` 2026-10-16 feat: add the family directory, naming `mnvttxkntyqv`
- `ypsvtsslrkss` 2026-10-16 feat: the family directory opening, naming `oonqmttzlwtk`
- `vputsqvzvstx` 2026-08-31 docs: re-sync our copy from the payload, naming `ummxpxvkqpuu`
- `ltqplmmzmsqn` 2026-08-31 docs: copy the folded set into the payload, naming `xspxusqnlsxp`
- `zxspvztyuwkv` 2026-08-31 docs: triage the three-way diff and the members' proposals, naming
  `ruvsvzoxplrk`
- `sqoptttmvkyo` 2026-08-31 docs: define the agent-files type and title grammar, naming
  `smnyzxztklus`
- `mmxnuskzyqvt` 2026-08-31 agent-files(adoption): from iiac-perf, zc-ring-x1, 2026-08-31
  opening, naming `ulnvkqsqkmrs`

The partner is a draft local to wink's work-repo, on no bookmark and never pushed, replaced by
what landed, wink's call 2026-11-06 to list them rather than publish them:

- `qulkqsywytxm` 2026-08-04 refactor: trapezoid-push + body-intro validation opening, naming
  `yqxnsurlwsrr`
- `wzrymrkvuxmk` 2026-07-20 refactor: extract push/state.rs, naming `qknonomzmytm`, which landed as
  `zmvmrxslqxsm`
- `kxnnttnrmwoo` 2026-07-20 chore: open merge close-out cycle, naming `ozvukmlnmyuu`

The `ochid:` is malformed: its value contains digits, so it is not a jj change id, and read as a git
SHA or its prefix it names no commit in either repo, the original work-repo's included:

- `mkqtvoknqzlp` 2026-04-13 fix: remove submodule from init/clone (0.31.1), naming `34b6c258817b`

change id, so the link from the work side resolves, and only this one, from the agent side, is
broken. We think `34b6c258817b` is the work commit's SHA before it was rewritten, authored

Not on the list, since they resolve: an 8 or 32 character change id. `trailers --update` makes a
work commit's into its 12, and `validate-desc` gives an agent commit's a note, the agent-repo never
being rewritten. Six agent commits carry one, and five work commits did before the rewrite.

I think it's the right handoff. It's what continuation notes are for, and it gives vc-x2 a clean start: its own agent-repo, its own sessions, and its own rules, the agent-files copied in with the seed. A few things make it work.

**Where the note lives.** Write it in vc-x2's `TODO.md`, in a commit after the seed, not in vc-x1's closing:
- In vc-x1's `TODO.md`, the next vc-x1 session would read it as its own.
- In the seed itself, the seed would no longer be a pure copy of vc-x1's tree.

The adopt commit, or one right after it, is the natural place. I can write into vc-x2 until its agent starts. After that, the rule is to message its agent and not write there.

**What the note has to carry.** The vc-x2 agent won't have this conversation. Most of the context is already in files it inherits, so the note can point instead of repeat:
- **Where the decisions are:** in vc-x2's `TODO.md > ## Closed`, which holds this cycle's finished block once it has landed: why vc-x2 is seeded, and the xtask decisions. The vc-x2 needs from rung 2 will be `## Todo` entries.
- **The order of work:**
  1. Rename to vc-x2, with its starting version your call.
  2. Workspace plus xtask.
  3. Point `[validate]`/`[install]` at `cargo xtask`.
  4. Delete the subcommands.
- **The tooling during the gap:** use the installed `vc-x1` until `vc-x2-dev` exists, so the agent-files' `vc-x1 …` commands are correct at first and change with the rename.
- **What's left open:** the trailer format, decided in vc-x2, with a vc-x1 rewrite "maybe someday".

**Two things that won't come across by themselves:**
- `custom.md` is untracked, so `git archive` leaves it out. vc-x2 needs its own if you want one.
- The `~/.claude/projects/` symlink for vc-x2 comes from the adopt, as in the test.

**The order from here:**
1. Finish this cycle: the rung-1 commit, rung 2 as the filing rung, the closing, and the Land.
2. Seed vc-x2 from the landed `main`. You create the two GitHub repos.
3. Adopt, write the note, commit, and push, each with your approval.
4. You start a new session in vc-x2, and its acquaint reads the note first.

I'll record the trailer deferral in this cycle's deliberation, in your words: maybe someday, after the format is decided.

The plain version: yes, finish vc-x1's cycle, make the plain copy, and leave vc-x2 a handoff note so a fresh session there takes over. Put the note in vc-x2 after the copy, not in vc-x1. Keep it short by pointing at the decisions vc-x2 already inherits. Remember that `custom.md` won't come along by itself.

### chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2

#### Problem

(wink + agent, 2026-11-06) vc-x1 is to be succeeded by vc-x2, seeded from vc-x1's tree without
history, and before it is seeded vc-x1 must be complete as the archive vc-x2 refers back to. It is
not:

- 659 of its 686 work commits carry `ochid:` alone, so their agent partner is not linked by SHA
  (`ocid:`) nor their parents (`pcid:`), and 2 carry no trailer. `trailers --update` stamps all
  three, but only for a range above the trunk, and it has never been run over a whole history.
- vc-x2, starting without history, reaches the why and how of its first tree only through vc-x1's
  history, and whether `lookup` can follow it there is untested.

#### Solution

Provisional:

- `vc-x1 trailers --update --range ..@-` rewrites the whole history automatically, rehearsed in a
  test repo made by `init --test-repo`, the code changed for the cases vc-x1's own history holds.
- A test vc-x2 is made from the rehearsal without history, its first commit naming vc-x1's final
  SHA by hand, and `lookup` is tried in it. What vc-x2 needs to reach vc-x1 is filed, not built.
- After the Land, outside the cycle: the backfill run on the real repos, the old `main` kept by a
  GitHub fork, `inksaville/vc-x1-original`, made before the rewrite is pushed, the rewrite pushed
  with wink's approval, and the final `main` tagged. vc-x1 is then complete and vc-x2 can be
  seeded.

#### Acceptance check

Provisional:

- In a fresh clone of the rehearsal's remotes, `vc-x1 validate-desc` passes over the whole history,
  and every work commit's `ochid:` and every agent commit's resolves.
- The dry run over `..@-` sorts every commit into rewritten, already current, or left with its
  reason, and none is left unexplained.
- In the test vc-x2, `lookup` reaches vc-x1's history for a sample of lines, by the hand-written
  link if need be, and what vc-x2 must build to do it properly is a Todo entry.

#### Deliberation

- Retitled, wink's (2026-11-06): the cycle opened as **make vc-x1 content agnostic**, from the Todo
  **Build config moves to an xtask**, and the deliberation moved that subject to vc-x2, leaving
  this cycle the completing of vc-x1. The Todo returned to `## Todo` unchanged.
- vc-x2 is seeded from vc-x1, wink's (2026-11-06): content agnostic, and its design is vc-x2's, not
  this cycle's. What was decided toward it, recorded so it is not lost:
  - vc-x1 knows the two repos and their links and nothing of a project's content, so `validate`,
    `build`, `install`, `run`, and the Land's install move to a `cargo xtask`, which runs vc-x1.
  - Seeded first, then xtask, wink's: the repo becomes a cargo workspace for the xtask, and every
    line of that work is vc-x2's, so vc-x1 stays the stable tool that manages it.
  - Named vc-x2 from its start, the agent's, so `vc-x2` and `vc-x2-dev` install beside `vc-x1` and
    never replace it.
  - Made without history, wink's, its first commit naming vc-x1's final SHA, the agent's, so
    provenance crosses the gap, and its agent-repo fresh.
  - Seeded, not forked, the agent's word with wink's agreement (2026-11-07): a GitHub fork shares
    its parent's whole history, and vc-x2 shares none, its first commit being a new root holding
    vc-x1's tree, made by `git archive` of vc-x1's `main`. Not a shallow clone, whose root keeps
    vc-x1's SHA with a missing parent, and which we think GitHub refuses as a push into an empty
    repo.
- `TODO.md` is left as it is, wink's (2026-11-06): its clean-up is vc-x2's, which inherits the file,
  so this cycle does not go down that hole.
- The whole history, wink's (2026-11-06): `trailers --update` over `..@-`, made fully automatic.
  - Automatic for vc-x1's 686 work commits, not for any history, the agent's bound: the dry run
    sorts every commit first, the code is changed only for the cases it shows, and a case that
    needs real design is filed for vc-x2.
  - The counts (2026-11-06): 659 `ochid:` alone, 25 current, 2 with no trailer, 46 merges.
- Rehearsed, then redone, the agent's: a test repo's remotes are local, so its trailers link by
  `file:///` URL and its history is never pushed. The real run repeats the rehearsal on the real
  repos after the Land, so it covers every commit, this cycle's included.
  - Every work SHA on `main` changes, and only the commit records: every tree is the same, the
    second rehearsal's 686 rewritten commits naming exactly the original 686 trees, so the files and
    the history's shape are unchanged. The rewrite of `main@origin` takes `--yes` and wink's
    approval.
  - No trailer names an old work SHA after the rewrite: an agent commit carries `ochid:` alone, a
    change id the rewrite keeps, and every rewritten `pcid:` names its new parent, all 686 in the
    second rehearsal. The old records are kept only for references from outside the trailers, the
    landmarks and SHAs in `notes/` and `TODO.md`, the messages' sha-links, the transcripts, and
    links posted elsewhere.
  - We think jj writes each rewritten commit's change id into its git header, so the change ids an
    agent commit's `ochid:` names survive a fresh clone. The rehearsal's fresh clone shows it.
  - The first rehearsal (2026-11-06): 683 commits rewritten in 35m41s, a rerun finding nothing. In
    its fresh clone `lookup` gave the same answer as the real repo for a sample of lines, since it
    follows `ochid:` change ids and never a URL, so `file:///` and `https://` links read alike.
  - Its errors, all older than the rewrite, wink's calls (2026-11-06): an older id form that
    resolves is made the 12 by `trailers` and is a note in `validate-desc`, the agent-repo's
    included, and what cannot resolve is a known list, its 3 unpushed drafts listed rather than
    published. A SHA naming one agent commit is made a change id the same way, wink's call.
  - The second rehearsal (2026-11-06), with the opening on its `main` and this rung's build: the
    dry run sorted all 686 commits, the run changed 686 in 36m42s, and a rerun found 686 current.
    In its fresh clone `validate-desc` reports an `err` or a `miss` for the known list's commits
    and no others, 1 and 2 on the work side, 15 and 1 on the agent side.
  - A tag on the old `main` makes every rewritten change divergent in a clone that fetches it,
    the agent's test (2026-11-06): the tagged original and the rewrite share a change id, so an
    `ochid:` naming it resolves to two commits. The old `main` is kept some other way, wink's to
    decide before the real run.
  - Kept by a GitHub fork, wink's (2026-11-07), tested on a throwaway pair: GitHub refuses a fork
    into the account that owns its parent, so the fork is made in a second account, `inksaville`,
    and renamed `vc-x1-original`. After a description rewrite and force-push of the parent:
    - Each old SHA opens at the parent's `/commit/<sha>` URL, with a banner saying it belongs to no
      branch, and at the fork's, and `git fetch origin <old-sha>` from the parent returns it.
    - A fresh `git clone` or `jj git clone` of the parent holds the new history alone, with no
      divergent change.
    - We think GitHub collects garbage per fork network, so the fork's `main` keeps the old records
      as long as the fork and the `inksaville` account exist, and a test minutes old cannot show
      it. Branch protection on the fork's `main` and a backed-up mirror are wink's options.
- `lookup`'s fixes lean vc-x2, wink's (2026-11-06), the agent's rule beside it: a fix that makes
  vc-x1 readable on its own history is vc-x1's, completing it, and one that crosses from vc-x2 into
  vc-x1 is vc-x2's, the only side with the gap.
  - The test vc-x2's link is hand-written, since vc-x2 does not yet read one, and its form is fixed
    before the real vc-x2 is made, a change after meaning a rewrite of vc-x2's first commit.

#### Rungs

The rung subsections, in the ladder's order. The ladder itself is in `zTOC.md > ## Ladder`.

opening was local, retitled it and returned the Todo it was opened from.

`trailers --update` has stamped ranges above the trunk, never a whole history with commits from

* An `ochid:` naming its partner in an older form was left as it is, with no `ocid:`.
  - One naming exactly one agent commit by an 8 or 32 character change id, or by a SHA, becomes
    its 12 character change id and gets its `ocid:`. The forms are told apart by jj's alphabets,
    `k` to `z` for a change id and hex for a SHA, and are 8 characters at least, so a marker such
    as `lost` is never read as one.
* A commit with no `ochid:` was skipped.
  - It gets its `pcid:` lines alone, so every commit links its parents. A Land, which stamps
    only the links a commit has, still skips it.
* A dry run over the trunk's remote was refused without `--yes`, and it ended in a count.
  - It runs, saying the real run takes `--yes`, and the summary sorts every commit: how many
    change, how many are current, each `ochid:` kept and why, and each commit with none.
* `validate-desc` made an older id an error though it names its partner.
  - An 8 or 32 character change id naming exactly one commit is a note, since the agent-repo is
    never rewritten and keeps the forms its commits were made with.
* What no change resolves is the known list, [vc-x1-history.md](notes/vc-x1-history.md): 16
  commits whose partner is gone, a draft never pushed, or named in a SHA's form that names
  nothing, and 3 with no trailer. The acceptance check reads "no error outside the list".
* The rewrite is quadratic, each describe rebasing the commits above it, and a linear one is
  filed in the backlog, the backfill being run once.
* The old `main` is kept by a GitHub fork in a second account, not a tag, which makes every
  rewritten change divergent, both tried and recorded in the deliberation.

##### chore: a test vc-x2 reaches vc-x1's history

Whether vc-x2, seeded without history, can reach the why and how of its first tree in vc-x1 is
untested. A test vc-x2 is seeded from the rehearsal, its first commit naming vc-x1's final SHA, and
`lookup` is tried in it, what vc-x2 needs being filed, a `seeded-from:` trailer among them.

##### chore: complete vc-x1, ready for vc-x2 closing

Closing out the cycle.

content.text:
I'd drop `pcid:` too. From your side, reading history on GitHub or in a clone, it adds nothing:

- **Parents:** git already records them, and GitHub shows them as links in every commit's header. `pcid:` repeats that in the message.
- **Repo identity:** its other job in the rationale was naming the work-repo inside a work commit. With `orepo:`, each side's partner names the other's repo, so that's covered.
- **Provenance across a copy:** the one case it uniquely handles is a commit copied into another repo. For vc-x2, that's one `seeded-from:` trailer on one commit, not a line on every commit.

And it works against the clean repos you want:
- It's the only trailer left that would hold a SHA. Any rebase, squash, or re-describe changes a parent's SHA, so every commit above it has a stale `pcid:` until it's restamped. That's the restamping the Land does today, and the cascade that made the backfill slow.

With both gone, **no trailer holds a SHA**. A description no longer depends on anything a rewrite changes, so rebasing, squashing, and squash-push leave every link valid. That's exactly what "both repos clean" needs.

**One rule that matters for squash-push:** a link survives a squash only if it names the change that's kept. `jj squash` from `@` into `@-` keeps `@-`'s change id and drops `@`'s. So an `ochid:` must name the commit being squashed *into*, never the one squashed away. That's the agent-side version of "a ladder is never squashed", and the new text should say it.

**On the `orepo:` format:**
- It holds the other repo's URL, normalized to https, or `file:///` for a test repo, the same as the URL part of `ocid:` today.
- One `orepo:` covers the `ochid:` lines after it. Your multi-work-repo case then works naturally: `orepo: A`, its `ochid:`s, then `orepo: B`, its `ochid:`s.
- Existing history keeps its `ocid:`/`pcid:` lines. validate-desc accepts them as an older form, the same way it treats older ids, so vc-x1 stays unrewritten.

**Scope.** This is bigger than a wording change, and it touches:
- **Code:** `vc-x1 commit` stamping; the Land's link pass; `trailers --update`, which would no longer have a cascade; validate-desc; and the `xxxx` placeholder going away.
- **Rules:** the `agent-data/jj.md` linking section, the "agent first" and mid-cycle backup bullets in AGENTS.md, and the rationale. Plus the agent-files version bump to v0.3.1-3.

Lookup is unaffected, since it reads only `ochid:`. I'd make it an inserted rung, after rung 1 and before rung 2, titled something like "feat: orepo replaces ocid and pcid". Rung 1, still under review, gets committed first.

Shall I go ahead that way, with `pcid:` dropped along with `ocid:`?

The plain version: yes, drop `pcid:` too. Git and GitHub already show parents, and it's the trailer that goes stale whenever history is rewritten. With `orepo:` plus `ochid:` and nothing else, no trailer holds a SHA, so both repos can be squashed and cleaned without breaking a link, as long as each link names the commit that's kept. I'd do it as its own rung, after committing rung 1.

I agree, and I'd make the rule simple: **the agent never pushes a trunk.** Here's why it's more than a matter of taste.

**The real flaw is the force-push of `main`, not the two pushes.** Two repos can never be pushed atomically, so that's true today as well. What your scenario adds:
1. The agent lands and pushes both `main`s.
2. The session keeps writing: my closing words, then the exit.
3. Your squash-push folds that tail into the agent-repo's tip and **force-pushes `main`**.

Anyone who fetched between steps 1 and 3 now has a `main` that was rewritten under them. A trunk should only ever move forward. Topic bookmarks are different: they're work in progress, and force-pushing them is normal.

**The agent-repo has no topic bookmark**, so the agent-repo needs the same treatment. Today "the agent-repo needs no bookmark", and a mid-cycle agent backup pushes straight to its `main`. Any later squash-push into that commit force-pushes `main` the same way. So under your rule, the agent either doesn't push the agent-repo at all, or pushes it to a WIP bookmark, for example the cycle's bookmark name, deleted at publish.

**What I'd propose:**
- **The agent may push:** work topic bookmarks, and the agent-repo only to a WIP bookmark. Both can be force-pushed freely.
- **The agent never pushes** `main` in either repo. Its Land is local: `vc-x1 land` without `--push`, plus the install. Its last words name the publish step instead of ending in "Published".
- **You publish after exiting:** squash-push the agent-repo first, so the change ids the work side names exist on the remote before anything names them, then push the work `main` and delete the topic bookmarks on the remote. Each `main` moves once, forward only.
- **We think one command should do that sequence,** say `vc-x1 publish`, proposed and not built. Until it exists, it's the two commands you run today.

This replaces two current rules: "Hard stop after the final push" (the agent no longer makes the final push) and the Land's publish step. It also simplifies "approval per push", since the pushes the agent still makes are all to rewritable work-in-progress bookmarks.

Should this go into the same inserted rung as `orepo:`, or into a rung of its own? I'd keep it in the same rung: it's what makes squash-push safe, and v0.3.1-3 would ship both together.

The plain version: the problem isn't two pushes, it's that the clean-up squash-push would rewrite a `main` that's already published. So the agent should land locally and push only work-in-progress bookmarks, and you publish both `main`s after the session ends, agent-repo first. That way each `main` only ever moves forward.

content.text:
Yes, it's possible, and I think it's the right guard. It also fits your framing better than my "the agent never pushes a trunk".

**The rule as you state it** is the current one: the agent publishes a Land only with your explicit approval, or under a waiver like "complete and publish these N cycles". Within such a run:
- After each `land --push`, the next step is `commit --opening`, and the session tail since the Land rides that opening's agent commit. Nothing is rewritten and no squash-push is needed.
- Without permission, the agent lands locally, and you publish after exiting: squash-push the agent-repo, then push work `main`. Each `main` moves forward once.

**The gap is the last Land of a delegated run.** It's published, and the session keeps writing after it. A squash-push there would force-push the agent `main`. So either the tail waits in the agent `@` for the next session's opening, which is today's at-rest state, or the delegation covers every Land but the last, and you publish that one. That's your choice for each delegation. The guard makes sure a mistake here gets refused instead of rewriting `main`.

**The `squash-push` guard.** It's a single check before anything changes: if the squash target (`@-` by default) is already in `::<bookmark>@origin`, the push would be forced, so refuse and change nothing. The same goes for an empty `@` whose bookmark isn't a fast-forward of `<bookmark>@origin`. The code already has what it needs (`jj::matches` with a revset).

Two things to know:
- **It reverses the command's original purpose.** Its module doc says it was built to rewrite the already-pushed agent commit, "so the push is a forced update", and its help names "a deliberate amend-and-push" on a work repo. I'd keep that as an explicit opt-in, `--force`, which is safe on a WIP topic bookmark and never the default.
- **`vc-x1 push` uses it internally** as its `squash-push-bot` stage. There the target is the agent commit just made and not yet pushed, so the guard doesn't trigger. The existing tests should confirm that.

So the inserted rung would hold three related changes under v0.3.1-3:
1. `orepo:` + `ochid:` replace `ocid:` and `pcid:`, with the old forms left unchecked.
2. Squash-push becomes the clean-up step, and the rule says a squash folds into the named commit.
3. `squash-push` refuses a forced push unless given `--force`.

Shall I commit rung 1 now and start that rung? Rung 1's review is still yours to close with "continue".

The plain version: yes. The agent publishes a Land only when you allow it, and a delegated run carries the leftover session data into the next cycle's opening. `squash-push` can easily check whether it would rewrite something already published and refuse unless you pass `--force`. That one check makes a mistaken clean-up impossible.

- The trailers, wink's (2026-11-07, decided 2026-11-09):
  - `ocid:` pins the agent commit's SHA, so an agent commit is never amended or squashed into, and

    parents, and makes a describe rewrite every commit above it.
  - Decided, an inserted rung: `orepo: <url-to-other-repo>` replaces `ocid:`, and with `ochid:`
    names exactly where the partner is. `pcid:` is dropped too, the agent's case and wink's
    agreement: git and GitHub already show the parents, `orepo:` names the repo, and a copied
    commit's provenance is vc-x2's one `seeded-from:`. No trailer then holds a SHA, so a rebase,
    a squash, or a squash-push leaves every link valid. Lost: GitHub's one click to the agent
    commit, plain git resolving the link, and the transcript pinned by a hash.
  - One `orepo:` covers the `ochid:` lines after it, so an agent commit naming partners in several
    repos groups them, `orepo: A`, its `ochid:`s, then `orepo: B`, the agent's.

86	    )]

106	/// Per-invocation squash-push inputs: the clap-free shape the op
107	/// works against. Built from `SquashPushArgs` at the binary edge

109	/// while `vc-x1 push`'s `squash-push-bot` stage constructs it
110	/// directly.

112	pub struct SquashPushParams {
113	    pub repo: PathBuf,
114	    pub squash: SquashSpec,
115	    pub bookmark: String,
116	    /// This run is the user's at-rest invocation rather than
117	    /// `vc-x1 push`'s `squash-push-bot` stage.
118	    ///
119	    /// Everything addressed to a person is gated on it: the
120	    /// publish-mismatch report, the precheck's and after-check's
121	    /// lines, and the prompt. Mid-push every one of them is wrong.
122	    /// The mismatch is the normal state there, since `bookmark-set`

129	    /// the `already sync'd` early return gave push before the

131	    pub at_rest: bool,

134	    /// opt-in. Resolved from `--yes`, then `--ask`, then the repo's

136	    pub yes: bool,

146	/// boolean flag cannot turn a configured `true` back off, which is
147	/// why `--ask` exists rather than a `--no-yes`.
148	pub fn resolve_yes(yes: bool, ask: bool, key_value: Option<bool>, default: bool) -> bool {
149	    if yes {

153	    } else {

163	fn config_yes(repo: &Path) -> Result<Option<bool>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {

196	        };

206	}

Sync(sync::SyncArgs),

    /// Squash SOURCE into TARGET, advance a bookmark, and push
    #[command(
        long_about = "Squash SOURCE into TARGET (defaults: SOURCE=@, TARGET=@-),\n\
        advance a bookmark, and push.\n\n\
        Captures a repo's trailing working-copy writes into the last\n\
        commit and publishes it: rewriting an already-pushed commit,\n\
        so the push is a forced update. Built for the bot repo\n\
        (`.claude`, the session tail), and useful on the work repo as\n\
        a deliberate amend-and-push.\n\n\
        Zero-ceremony default: bare `vc-x1 squash-push` squashes\n\
        @ -> @- in `.` and pushes the bookmark of the line you are\n\
        on. With an empty `@` but work still to do, the squash is\n\
        skipped and the push still runs.\n\n\
        --bookmark defaults to the line's own bookmark, the nearest one\n\
        at or above the squash target, and there is no literal\n\
        default. On the agent repo that is `main`. On a work repo\n\
        running a cycle it is the topic bookmark, so a bare run\n\
        publishes the line you are working and never advances `main`.\n\
        Several candidates, or none, is an error asking you to name\n\
        one, since a wrong guess here publishes something. Every\n\
        argument is a flag: the old positional is refused, naming\n\
        --bookmark.\n\n\
        A precheck asks whether the run has work at all: the working\n\
        copy at rest, the bookmark at its origin, and the bookmark\n\
        already at the squash target. That third condition is there\n\
        because a bookmark behind its target has a commit to publish\n\
        even when it matches origin. A run with no work prints\n\
        `<label>: clean` and exits 0 having touched nothing, <label>\n\
        being the repo's directory name. Every other run prints the\n\
        same line after the push, as a report only: the exit code\n\
        says whether the push completed, not what that line found.\n\n\
        With work found, the run acts without asking, the default\n\
        `squash-push.yes` sets. --ask turns the prompt on for one run\n\
        and -y/--yes turns it off. With the prompt on, a non-tty run\n\
        is an error rather than a hang, and declining is an error too.\n\n\
        As `vc-x1 push`'s squash-push-bot stage it says nothing and\n\
        asks nothing, there being no one mid-push to read a line or\n\
        answer a prompt. The precheck's decision still applies, so a\n\
        stage with no work still does nothing."
    )]
    SquashPush(squash_push::SquashPushArgs),
